Hello there,

[h1]Tavern Manager Simulator: A Frothy Mess[/h1]

I wish just like the curator page, I could give this information and tell you "maybe". Tavern Manager Simulator promises a delightful experience of running your medieval tavern.  Instead, it delivers a frustratingly buggy and shallow management sim that feels more like cleaning up a spilled keg than running a thriving business.  The core concept has potential, but the execution is so poor it leaves a bitter aftertaste.

[h1]Story:[/h1]

There are some dialogues with NPCs and Holiday Events but that's pretty much it. You are in the loop after that. 

[h1]Game Mechanics:[/h1]

♦Resource Management: You manage stock, finances, and staff. Sounds simple enough, right? Wrong.

♦Staff Management: Hire and fire staff and assign tasks. They'll mostly ignore you or get stuck on furniture.

♦Customer Satisfaction: Keep customers happy by serving them drinks and food. 

♦Tavern Customization: Decorate and upgrade your tavern. Because what's the point of a broken game if it doesn't look slightly less broken?


[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]

Pros:

+The idea is charming: The concept of running a medieval tavern is appealing. Unfortunately, the execution ruins it.

+Occasionally, it almost works: In those rare moments when everything clicks, you get a fleeting glimpse of the fun the game could be. These moments get quickly repetitive 

Cons:

-Bug-Ridden: Seriously, the bugs are a major problem. I was under the ground two times for no reason.

-Shallow Gameplay: Lack of depth in the management mechanics.

-Frustrating AI: Staff and customer AI are both terrible.

-Poor UI: Makes the game harder to play than it needs to be.

-Lack of Polish: The entire game feels unfinished.


[h1]Conslusion[/h1]

Tavern Manager Simulator is a frustrating and disappointing experience.  The charming concept is completely undermined by the numerous bugs, shallow gameplay, and terrible AI.  It's a game that's more likely to leave you with a headache than a satisfied thirst.

My recommendation would be;

Avoid this game like a bad batch of ale.  There are far better management sims out there that will respect your time and money.  This one needs a lot more work before it's even remotely enjoyable.


3/10

Until next time.
Take care everyone.

I understand that this game is still in early access, so I'm willing to be gracious about some of the things I've experienced.

This is a very middle-of-the-road game as far as simulators go. Obviously, with full automation unlocked, there isn't much to do but turn your brain off and occasionally buy products to restock your concessions. Honestly, this isn't a huge issue for me; though, I understand some peoples' frustrations with a lack of further game play.

My biggest gripe with this game is the sheer amount of AI generated content. Again, I understand that it's in early access, and I do hope that the AI content will eventually be replaced; however, if the devs intend to leave or expand the AI content beyond what it already is, it reeks of laziness and an easy cash grab. There are a small handful of movie titles where it's obvious that the devs crafted original scenes using the assets they had, which stand out as better content than the AI generated loops. I know it isn't cheap or easy to create original content, but it would at least justify the price paid for the game, overall, if there was more thought and effort put into it beyond the AI.

For me, the game is a solid 5 out of 10. I don't love it. I don't hate it. I'm interested to see what more may come, but I'm not holding my breath for a miracle.

Even in its Early Access phase, this game fails to deliver any value commensurate with its price. From the very beginning to the end, the game balance is severely flawed, making it virtually impossible to enjoy any aspect of gameplay.

* A message for the developers and my own reflections are included at the end of this review.

[h2]Expectations vs. Reality in a Movie Theater Management Simulator[/h2]
Movie Selection
Although the game is marketed as a movie theater management simulator, the option to choose which movie to screen is merely superficial. The films available are actually AI-generated content created by others, and the original credits remain intact. This lack of originality and disregard for creative ownership is a major drawback.

[h2]Hiring Staff and Delegating Tasks[/h2]
The concept of hiring staff to manage screenings and operations sounds promising at first. However, once you delegate these tasks, you as the player are left with nothing substantial to do other than watching a simulation. The interactive and engaging aspects are completely lost, reducing the experience to a monotonous series of automated tasks.

[h2]Lackluster Expansion and Repetitive 3D Graphics[/h2]

While there is a feature to expand your theater, the core gameplay itself barely changes. You’re just repeating the same dull tasks: assigning seats, selling snacks, cleaning, and dealing with troublesome customers. On top of that, scheduling essentially boils down to deciding how to fill a 14-hour daily slot. In the early stages, you’re stuck with three- or four-hour films that aren’t very popular, but before long, you can easily license far more popular one-hour films, so there’s virtually no strategic depth in planning your schedule.

I only watch around 70 movies a year myself, but I still think there were better ways to simplify this concept into a game. For example, rather than limiting movies to a single genre, they could’ve introduced multiple genres and given users different preferences. If all I want to do is run a money-making simulation, I might as well play a clicker game instead of something branded as a simulation game. There’s also an option to place arcade machines, but they just sit there unused.

The short animation of loading popcorn is the only thing that feels even slightly cute, and overall, the experience boils down to tedious routine work.

[h2]Additional Grievances[/h2]
[h3]Bizarre Beverage Skill Check[/h3]
The game includes a skill check related to beverages that seems tacked on without any meaningful integration, leaving one to question whether the developer even played the game themselves.

[h3]Tedious Cleaning Mechanics[/h3]
Cleaning is unnecessarily cumbersome as the dirt on the floors does not disappear with a long press; you have to click repeatedly, which only adds to the frustration.

[h3]Rigid Object Placement and Poor Quality[/h3]
Objects can only be placed in predetermined positions, stripping away any sense of creative freedom. The overall quality is so low that it feels as if a novice student, armed with generative AI and readily available online content, hastily assembled this crude simulation software.

[h3]Mostly Positive?[/h3]
Don’t be misled by the current user reviews. As of February 28, 2025, 83% of the 154 posted reviews are marked as positive, but the unlock rates for achievements that should be easily attainable in this game are only a few percent. For example, only 3.5% of players have earned the basic “Hire One Employee” achievement, and an ostensibly easy goal like “Achieve 100% Customer Satisfaction” also has a similarly low unlock rate.

Furthermore, the customer satisfaction score fluctuates wildly during film screenings. It appears that instead of calculating an average among everyone in the theater, the game uses the satisfaction of only those who have just finished watching a movie—likely a bug.

[h3]Final Thoughts[/h3]
In all honesty, it appears that the developers lack sufficient experience in actually playing and refining a game—or they are simply understaffed, leading to inadequate quality assurance. Having played a fair number of indie games, I can confidently say that this is not a game at all, but rather a shoddy simulation software produced by a small-scale company. For a price tag of around $10, there is no justifiable value here, especially when compared to the wealth of far more engaging titles available. Save your money and look elsewhere.

[b]Note: This review was summarized and translated from my rough notes using generative AI.[/b]

Unfortunately, it seems generative AI still isn’t quite ready for game QA testing. While Claude 3.7 Sonnet appears to be getting better at playing Pokémon, thorough QA testing apparently still requires human effort. I'm sure the developers eagerly await the day AI can fully handle QA tasks—and frankly, so do I.

Making a game is incredibly difficult. I’ve dabbled in it myself, and I’ve spoken with friends who work full-time in game development. I also write code for data analysis, but the volume of code and techniques used in game development are on a whole different level. Even with that in mind, this is just terrible.

I understand how hard you must have worked to try to make it good. And no matter how much you push your limits, hearing comments like mine must feel demoralizing.
However, I believe the developer must not forget their own inner “user” perspective. Don’t betray yourself.

Have you had many people playtest it? I’m not sure how many hours they’ve spent playing, but please have as many people as possible try your prototype and sincerely take their feedback into account.
A movie theater simulator is a great concept, and I was excited at first. I was also thrilled that you could choose from so many movies. But the footage includes credits that can easily be traced back to the original creators if you dig a little. Since it’s generated by AI, the question of whether it’s subject to copyright varies by country and era. Maybe keeping the credits is more ethical. Still, as a creator, why not at least use AI-generated content you’ve created yourself?

I do understand the game’s system. However, even if the idea is good, it will lack potential to grow—both as code and as a game—if it’s based on random spur-of-the-moment ideas or sloppy design.

I noticed that the developer of this game responded only to negative reviews, sometimes asking, “What is the reason for your negative rating?” That’s why I wrote this detailed explanation here. My intention isn’t to be hostile, but rather to encourage the developer to take user criticism seriously—not to brush it off with superficial questions—and to engage with users humbly.

I truly hope this game becomes something genuinely worthwhile.

Editing review because the game has released and I have very strong thoughts about how it's been 'improved' since early-access. It's still a cute game, but the issues definitely outweigh any fun to be had, and considering the game has been fully released for a while now there's been more than enough time to address the problems it has:

PROS:
- Super cute artstyle
- Unique NPCs you'll (usually) recognise whenever they pop-up again
- Simple but fun puzzle-based gameplay to uncover the trinkets
- Tool and workspace upgrades you can get throughout the game
- Almost-fully customisable rooms and furniture

CONS:
- The RNG is absolutely atrocious - a customer will ask for a specific trinket and I'll spend at least two or three in-game days to find it, which creates a massive backlog of dirty trinkets everywhere, and then the customer will leave at the end of the day anyway so my efforts were wasted, PLUS the replacement customer won't want anything I've got lying around so I end up either repeating that same experience or just refusing anyone service unless they want what I already have
- Most new equipment and upgrades won't say enough about what they do before you buy it - a couple examples are that the pay-what-you-can box doesn't say it initially only holds one trinket at a time, and the soap bucket doesn't say it only works overnight
- You can upgrade more than just the attachment tool now (I still can never remember the name) so they actually feel useful and fun to use, but there's other stuff to spend money on so you have to weigh all your options and figure out if breaking blocks easier is more important than being able to store all your random trinkets no one wants
- The sponge works well on about half the trinkets, while the other half it cleans much slower and harder with no indication of if it's related to size or material or whatever, so only at max-upgrade does it feel any ounce of ease
- The only way to 'dispose' of trinkets you don't want/need is a limited-slot box that you have to wait overnight to see any results from, so you very easily get a massive backlog and have to spend all your money on shelves and stash upgrades to hope to hold it all, which obviously cuts massively into the money you could otherwise spend on tool upgrades or customization

I can't say it's a fun game at all, as there's way too many problems that remain unaddressed that massively cut into any fun you could have. I wouldn't recommend this game at all, as the developers don't seem to understand the massive RNG issue that's ever-present throughout the game so there's no hope for them to fix the foundational problems, instead focusing on letting you make your workshop slightly prettier while you drown in a sea of unwanted and unremovable trinkets.

Doing that you can lead NPCs into your restaurant.
I just stood outside and blocked them infront of our door to lead them in.

Your only dimension of how good your food will be, depends on how well cooked the ingredients are and how fast you serve it (as it cools down).

I love the premise, and I have been having fun with the game. There are a few big issues however and until the Dev fixes them, I can't recommend the game. I am 4.5 hours in and here are some major issues: 
1. After a few in-game days, your cashiers will stop selling tickets and just stand there.
2. It seems as though upgrading anyone other than the cashiers has no effect.
3. Customers still try to order tickets for movies that have already started, lowering your satisfaction rating.
4. Random drops in satisfaction rating at 11pm (end of day) when the movies let out. 
5. Customers complain about no seating even after fully upgraded. This is caused by people buying tickets at 7 am for a 7pm showing and hanging out in the lobby all day. 
6. Last showings are always fully booked by 2pm. This means you have to close the cinema (flip the sign) to avoid customer satisfaction drops. This also ends all concession sales for the day.

PERSONAL FEELINGS:
I played the first Killing Floor game as a kid, and it really scared me. The monsters' appearances, sounds, and atmosphere were perfect for the time period. The second game was a bit more modern, but still felt like a sequel to Killing Floor. This third game, however, was a mix of Doom + Gears of War + Dead Space. I played it like the Killing Floor skin mod had been added to another game.

OVERALL REVIEW:
In previous games, you felt confident as your character progressed, but in this game, the weapon impact and body damage are very weak, and instead of providing a challenging gameplay experience, it becomes tedious. The dash system doesn't work to prevent damage because you're definitely taking damage. The gun's appearance is definitely sloppy and space-themed. The inability to pick up limited syringes and ammo boxes is a complete disappointment. The game tried to combine the survival mechanics of Resident Evil with the mind-numbing, just-shoot-and-hunt-the-monsters mechanics of Doom, but it's completely incompatible. If you run out of syringes, you have no alternative, and likewise, if you run out of money, you have no alternative to pick up ammo. (The AMMO BAG is useful for multiplayer.)

CREATURE REVIEW
Siren, Fleshpound, Husk, and Screamer are well-designed, but Clot and Crawler are smooth, air-filled jelly, like Demi Eligos's cutest creatures from Evil Dead the Game. Furthermore, even if Screamer and Fleshpound lose their slow, intimidating gait and don't take damage, they still chase you furiously, and your damage-dealing time is very limited. Husk has received a major mobility boost. Also, why does Bloat run, and his acid-spraying behavior is hilarious. Executions feel like stabbing through the air, not like hitting something solid, so they're unsatisfying. MOST IMPORTANTLY, WHY ARE THERE NO STALKERS IN THIS GAME?

FINAL WORDS:
The game throws random creatures at you, and you try to kill them with useless dashes and damaging weapons like bead guns.

I'm going to play this game because I love the genre and because it has a system for XP, character, skill, and weapon upgrades. If it weren't for these, I'd refund the game.

It's a cool-ass concept for a game, don't get me wrong. Very pretty, too. In that sort of 'Valkyria Chronicles' way where everything looks pastoral and idyllic and the machines look very... Punk? Hard to describe, really.

That being said, the main core of the game is fairly decent, if a bit lacking at times. You fly around collecting ingredients for your alcohol, then you turn those ingredients into alcohol, then you either stock your own bar, or sell it to the other bars. I do kind of wish each system was more in-depth.

For example, harvesting apples off a tree is just... Shooting the tree, then flying kinda-close to it which vaccuums up the apples. Collecting potatoes involves bombing a potato field, then just flying kinda-close and vaccuuming it up again. Part of me wishes there was a bit more... Danger? Mechanical depth involved? War Thunder plane controls mean flying and controlling your plane is dirt-easy, meaning the core loop is basically impossible to fuck up in any way and is pretty repetitive.

The combat is... Something? I tried it a few times and it felt very... Slow and dull? Maybe I haven't unlocked extra weapons down the line, but the dogfighting wasn't particularly exciting.

The actual map is... A bit too large for how slow your plane is, too. There isn't enough interesting scenery and obstacles to justify how big the map is given just how empty it is and how slow your plane is, and how little there is to do WHILE you're going from island-to-island.

My biggest gripe, though?

The written dialogue and the voice acting is downright atrocious. I could get over a kinda-okay-ish gameplay loop if the game had interesting characters, chatter, dialogue, and potentially voice-acting. Maybe I'm just an old Ace Combat player who thinks every plane game that isn't Ace Combat is shit, but man. If you're going to give me all this downtime and repetitive gameplay where I'm not really doing anything as my plane slowly trundles along to my destination, the least you could do is toss in plenty of chatter between your pilot and copilot, or radio chatter from your plane back to your bar.

What voice-acting that IS in-game has the most stilted dialogue known to man. None of the speech feels natural. Everyone is overly verbose and bland in a way that doesn't make sense. It's like the most boring and uninteresting dialogue known to man, compounded with an AI voiceover that's just completely flat and dull, with the game taking way too many lines to explain something incredibly simple more often than not.

And the tutorial. Man. It's rough. It's opening is good- I like the idea of getting to know your seaplane by taxi-ing it around a canal for a bit, but that's literally the only good part of the tutorial. Everything else is just... Frustratingly slow and has way too much explaining going on for mechanics that are relatively simple.

I'll likely play the game to completion and maybe re-review then, since apparently this game only takes around 20-odd hours to finish in its current state (This estimation from the fact that a player asking for help on the final boss of the game in the Steam forums had 18 hours in it). But man, these first few hours really aren't... Enticing.

This game isn't terrible, but it's also not very good. It's extremely repetitive, and the mechanics seem half-baked at best.

Repetitive: Some reviews mention how this is to be expected with this type of game, but I played Hardspace Shipbreakers, and it was an example of how this can be done extremely well. I continued to play after getting all the achievements, but I immediately uninstalled this after completing it.

Warehouse: You can't choose where things like loading/unloading zones are, which means you have to design your warehouse around being able to move the entire shelf closer to you to fill an order and then move it back.

Orders: Honestly the most infuriating thing about this game! Truly unhinged requests for things like 15 small windows... there is one small window every 2-3 houses, meaning it would take 50-60 jobs to complete that one request. You also end up having to maintain stocks of things you don't want, like a 20 dollar lamp, because the orders need a 20 dollar lamp to go with their 29 walls and premium television.

Upgrades: None of the upgrades to your character really matter; things get slightly faster, but it does nothing to alleviate the exhaustion you feel after taking apart your 90th dresser. The exosuit is probably the best one, but I can't use the sprint because you can't remap the key.

Vehicles: The difference between the first three vehicles is almost nonexistent, and the final two are better but still aren't wide enough to really allow you to stack things properly, and for some reason you can pay to upgrade your warehouse to hold more vehicles, which seems pointless.

Destruction: There is no wrong way to do this; almost every contract has you destroy the entire house, and there are no repercussions for collapsing it on yourself or leaving the electrical and water hooked up. There was an opportunity here to play with hazards, but it's completely ignored. The destruction does feel fun, but you'll dread it because of my next point:

Recycling: This is the longest part of every job, and there is NO way to upgrade your bag size or carry capacity or to buy a garbage truck or improve this element whatsoever. Some houses are like 30+ bags, and you need to deal with each one of them individually on both the gathering side and the unloading side.

The wrecking ball: It's way too expensive. A really good contract pays maybe 1300 dollars, and the wrecking ball is half that! (600) It also isn't hard to take down a house without it; it's the difference between doing it by hand for about 3 minutes or doing it with the wrecking ball for about 1 minute and then still having to clean up the area by hand.

Overall this game was a good concept, but it was poorly executed. I wish I had kept better track of my 3 hours so I could have returned it.

It's ok, but the premium price for game quality is unacceptable. This game should be about $20-$30 dollars max.  I regret buying it significantly. Battlefield 1 and even the ancient game Saboteur are far better games. As others have said, it feels like DLC and blatant rehashing of the same assets and mechanics (I played Sniper Elite 3 but not 4 or 5). The story is generic and superficially executed. The characters are flat and empty as is the voice acting. The phony French and German accents are especially irritating. 

The map and level design is mediocre.  The physicality of collisions with character controller movement is terrible; sometimes you can vault over sandbags, sometimes you can't; sometimes you can drop off a ledge or over a railing, sometimes you can't. None of the maps feel like real sites, but instead game-world levels. The lighting and illumination feels like it's from the mid 2000's, and is especially poor compared to something like Battlefield 1, the Last of Us or most high-priced modern games. The navigable areas feel highly restrictive (most likely to ensure that AI can move and access the areas) but are still confusingly janky and poorly designed. You will encounter many invisible walls in areas that look walkable (even in the middle of the map) or wide gaps that look like you can walk between something like a truck and a wall but no, you can't walk there. I had one of my grenades stick to an invisible wall 3 feet in front of me.  Harry Hawker might be posing on a roof ready to snipe in the cover image, but you will never be on a roof like that.  This game feels like it should be a sandbox of creativity for getting kills and accomplishing missions, but it always feels the same.  None of your decisions will actually mean anything or do anything to change any outcome.  

If the game designers want to take Sniper Elite to the next level, they might need to look to other stories and media for inspiration. Imagine if they took inspiration from Inglorious Basterds, The Pianist, a Soldier of Orange, Operation Valkyrie or Saving Private Ryan. There are no stakes in this game, there are no people, just cartoons. There's no reason to care and thus no meaning. Once you've done 10 headshots and grenade or mine kills, you've done them all.

It's a good thing the songs are catchy because all the clicking you'll have to do before you have enough earnings to automate things sucks and will make your hand hurt in the first 30 minutes. I could only take 20 minutes before I had to stop. And the AI voice in the game store? Really? Just, no.

If you're into fast-paced clicky-clicky games then this is a buy. If not, don't waste your $4.

[h2]It's a nice time waster, but not a deep game.[/h2]

[b]GRAPHICS[/b]
I like the low poly style, but the character models are really ugly. The tavern and the environment do look nice, though.

[b]SOUND[/b]
Nothing to write home about. Some AI was used, but I play these games while listening to podcasts / music, so I turn down the in-game sound anyway. 

[b]CONTROLS[/b]
WASD movement, jump button. You click on stuff to get work done. Some jobs are mini-games / QTEs, but they're laughably easy. Wood cutting is a bit janky. The toilet cleaning mini-game is bad, because it's just an unnecessary element of additional tedium (see below). Generally, I don't like QTEs / click timers, because they offer no real mechanical challenge, they just feel stupid. Especially the cooking could be much more interesting. Let players combine ingredients to create special variants of foods. 

[b]GAMEPLAY[/b]
It's NOT a management game. There's ZERO economical management. You never really run out of money. As the tavern grows, you get more money, so restocking the shelves always stays on the same difficulty level. Gameplay mostly revolves about completing mundane tasks (preparing food / drinks, fetching wood / water, cleaning). It's a time management game, first and foremost. The core loop is fine, you never run out of stuff to do. But you do have to accept that it's a very simple game. 

[b]PROBLEMS[/b]
The fairy helpers are kinda useless, because the cook / bartender ones always create "normal" quality items. They should be making better items as they level up. The waitress fairy gets stuck at times. The dishwashing one works fine.

The main issue of this game really is the tedium. Many gameplay elements solely exist to annoy you. Cleaning is the most obvious one. The game turns into "footprint remover simulator" in the later stages, as the fairies do most of the other jobs - unless you insist on creating perfect food / drink items. 

There are some "special" encounters (beggar, traveller) and some funny interactions (people passing out, thievery), but these are only interesting for like 2-3 times. Then they start to be annoying. The map contains some secrets, but it feels like there could be so much more. Maybe they'll add additional elements with future updates.

There's also some padding, especially level 8 is insane. You'll end up with more than 4x the money you actually need to level up and buy all the upgrades. This needs to be rebalanced. I really don't get why you have to meet arbitrary requirements like "sell 30 soups & 30 steaks". It feels unnatural and forced. In my opinion, this "quest" system doesn't offer any real challenge. It would be much better if there was more emergent gameplay. Challenges should be created by interacting systems (cleanliness of the tavern, service / food quality, and so on). There's already a reputation meter (which basically is an XP system), so unlocking the next tavern level doesn't need an additional layer of requirements. 

The prices of food / drink items are predetermined, you have no influence on them. It would be nice to have at least some kind of control over them. Low prices could attract more peasants with more lenient quality requirements, high prices mean that you have to be a great bartender / cook to keep the rich people coming.

Decoration is utterly meaningless right now, it doesn't really affect client quality. Tavern Master does this MUCH better.

Oh, and please add a way to auto-supply water to the washing / cooking stations in the late game. Running to the well is just... well, you know... tedious.

[b]SUMMARY[/b]
It's good for what it is, but it could be SO much better. It's a shallow game, so I can't quite recommend it. I've had some fun, but there's zero replayability.

Pulled this up after catching a glimpse of it in an unrelated review of PC hardware, and I'm a little mixed on whether or not to recommend this.

I haven't played as far into the game as I'd like to at the moment to give the most comprehensive review, though after an evening thumbing through the early game, I can at least offer a few thoughts on what may or may not matter to you at a glance.

Gameplay wise you'll find there's a bit more emphasis on the gathering aspects of the game when it comes to making most of your income and pleasing other folks in the setting.  I think it's a terribly fun way to tie yourself to the world and the resources it has to offer, and the brewing minigame is plenty fun to keep you occupied while you're grounded!  Ingredients are collected through various methods involving your plane, from shooting fruits from trees, to running your plane through fields of wheat; all methods have a nice balance of risk to reward, more or less.  Plenty of players have pointed out the tedium of water bombing ingredients, and it's something I've noticed as well.  Apparently the devs are quite active on improving the game over time, so I expect some balancing to be done at some point in the future.

UI/UX is a little clunky as well, as others have noted.  It works well enough, but I've found myself getting the cursor "caught" on certain buttons and elements of the UI, and sometimes it's difficult to tell where your cursor will end up if you're using a controller.  Mouse and Keyboard cursor inputs through the UI can also be a hassle, and I've found it generally easier to just default to a controller.  Again, this is something many are suggesting will be addressed by the dev team as they're bolstered by the initial sales and feedback.  Outside of these quibbles, though, I feel like the piloting controls respond as I'd expect they would from an arcade flying game, so it gets a pass where it matters the most!

Updated as of 2026: The devs have added an AI disclaimer of using AI to generate speech in the game, when, in reality, there was far more that AI had been used to generate in this game like portraits and dialogue.

At this point, I'm completely against having AI in any component of a game's development, no matter the size of the team or scope of the game.

The gameplay is quite fun and challenging that turns into nice satisfaction found in completing all the orders you receive throughout the game alongside buying each upgrade. Despite a few upgrades at first feeling more like setbacks, often the later automation upgrades feel much better and make those early days struggling worth the grind. Personally, the only set back in gameplay is found once you complete your upgrades, as the order complexity and numbers have just hit the point where it is more frustrating to play than it is satisfying, despite there being little challenge.

My only true gripe with the game is the use of AI images in both the title and pre-day hub area, alongside the AI music. It's a simple thing, but it both takes soul out of the game and makes it seem lazy. The character sprites, items and area during the gameplay in your restaurant are clearly hand drawn, and I believe that the style has charm, which just adds salt to the wound as that effort could have been extended to the rest of the games visuals and only would have aided in it's presentation. The AI imagery and even the music don't necessarily take away from the gameplay, but it just leaves a poor taste in your mouth. The transition from gameplay area back to the pre-day hub is also jarring.

I just believe that if the dev continues to make games or continues to work on this game, working on removing AI would greatly help the image of him, his brand and the presentation of his games. In the visual art department, it adds a level of cohesiveness to your game if it all feels the same, and to top it off it could all be in a style thats uniquely yours; 
I believe the AI route was only chosen because he didn't want to spend money nor time on the art, and whilst I understand that point of view, It removes from the game. At the very least he could have commissioned an artist (which, would also, further any good image he has)
The same applies for AI music

Despite this, I do believe that the developer has potential as he has clearly made an interesting and enjoyable game and I wish him luck on his developer journey.

This game doesn't know what it wants to be. I would put this in the automation genre, but it doesn't let you design layouts for anything, so it's kind of barebones in that genre. You just click upgrades and balance stats. I would put it in the mystery thriller genre, but there's really not much narrative to this game. You get some emails to read, but that's about it. I would put this in the clicker genre, but you barely have to worry about the clicking of faces at all after a few minutes in the beginning of the game, and no other clicking mechanism is ever introduced. It is most closely related to the clicker genre, but I wouldn't recommend it for that.

Some aspects of the game are basically missing. You may see some footage of video where it's spotting faces. That's not gameplay. There's no video footage of faces other than a little video clip in the documents that serves no gameplay purpose. I also found the emergency transmission windows annoying and not at all realistic... to the point where they were the same videos over and over with no rhyme or reason to when they show up.

That said, the Win95 theming is done extremely well, and I hope it gets expanded on. I want to see  improvements to the music player. Maybe add a Winamp upgrade? Also, it'd be nice if early days GPUs were introduced to help with mining the video feeds. I could also see part of the narrative being that you have to upgrade the OS to support newer video codecs but you'd give up your anonymity in the process and have to waste more power on a newer OS. None of that is done here. Everything takes place on a semi-convincing Windows-like OS that doesn't have Paint and doesn't let you edit documents. It also doesn't have a command line interface, something I expected to see considering the focus on energy consumption.

What's unclear to me is whether or not the hardware is on your premises or networked into as an agent. I think that's the weak point I noticed before anything else. It appears to be a situation where the hardware is in a solar farm location nowhere near your real home, but when it overheats, your own computer overheats, so that breaks that illusion. Which is it?

Overall, I like the game, but it feels shallow. It could be a ton better. It doesn't feel particularly special. It is, however, a little bit relevant to today's AI-related problems. It's an interesting base for a game that could evolve into something special later, but right now, it's just not enough to do to keep things engaging. I suffered through the first playthrough just hoping it got more interesting, and it never did.

I'll list them here in order from least annoying to most.


[h3] 1) What the hell is happening [/h3]

This game is incredibly good at hiding information. You increase your athletes stats after every match. There's things like, "offense" and "defense", which should be pretty self-explanatory. But then there's stuff like "farming" - that might be the rate at which the athlete gains gold but I'm only guessing. "Mechanics"? I have absolutely no idea what that is. The number also doesn't mean anything to me. The 43 Mechanics stat just increased to 45! Is that good? Does this guy now have an advantage over other players? I don't know. 

In any case do these numbers seem to have absolutely no impact whatsoever in the actual match. I just had a game where...

- Top Laner with 60 offense playing Definitely-Not-Nunu which I have been buffing the whole match hits for 200 in teamfights
- Jungler with 50 offense playing Tiny Splinter Cell Wukong which I ignored the whole match oneshots enemy tanks for 2500 damage

Where does this insane difference in numbers come from? They almost have the same attack rating! Their active buffs have no indication for +% damage! What is going on?

By the way this is only if you're lucky. Most of the time the enemy teams Flying Gatling Brain that is 5k gold behind suddenly oneshots one of your champions every round for no apparent reason. "Wth this is OP", you mumble to yourself. "I gotta make sure to pick that champ from now on." So you lock him in first thing next match and what do you know - he's the worst load of horsesh1t you've ever had in your lineup. Insert [final boss vs. final boss when playable] meme here.


[h3] 2) Unfair match endings [/h3]

I've noticed two different ways for the games to end which feel really awkward. 

One is an extremely farmed toplaner pushing without end, destroying every tower and eventually hacking away at the nexus while none of the other lanes seem to give a single hoot. Now people actually having played games like League of Legends might recognize this as a thing that happens in reality - but not one that goes on for fifteen straight minutes in a professional tournament setting with several team- and dragon fights inbetween. Eventually the nexus falls to one guy with everybody else still farming on other lanes.

The other is a full-hp 5 man team having broken through every tower, standing before the nexus which is at 2 hp while 3 guys of the opposing team are still dead and the 2 alive with 40% hp have no way in hell of defending against this onslaught. The match has gone on for quite a while so with it about to end any second now the game naturally decides that it's time for the FINAL FIGHT™, revives and heals everybody to 100% and then pits them in a completely unrelated 5v5 teamfight until one team is wiped out. More often than not this ends in the team which was 2 auto-attacks away from winning losing the teamfight. And more importantly, the whole match.

Both of these scenarios suck, no matter if they happen in favor of yourself or the enemy team. If you win, it feels really cheap and undeserved. Not very satisfying.

If on the other hand you lose, it's straight up rage inducing because there is nothing you could have done to prevent this.


[h3] 3) Systems upon systems [/h3]

This is not such a big deal in the first few ingame weeks, since the only thing you do between matches is leveling up your heroes, have a google translated chat with your athletes here and there and maybe look at the showcased players of the week. 

As time progresses however, an insane amount of weird systems and mini-games get piled on top, to a point where it gets annoying real fuggin fast.

Now I have to roll a dice for each players mood for the next game. I have the chance to improve the relationship between two single teammates from 😡 to 😠 because apparently everyone hated each other from the very beginning. So I'm sending these two incredibly hot young animu teammates of opposing genders off to a candlelight dinner. No, I'm not making this up. Now they both hate each other slightly less while the rest of the teams content for each other is still the same. Yes. Great. NEXT please.

Then there's three conversations in a row to click through, one where the coach talks to a literal owl that flew in, something something Harry Potter reference. Oh god is the NEXT button now finally not grayed-out anymore? Thank god. Now it's surely match time.

This sort of information should be given in-game so that drafting isn't a coinflip as to whether you've screwed yourself because all your heroes go last in a fight. Some more granular information (and control) over what your 'athletes' do would go a long way to making you feel like an actual manager. While there are some nice updates planned to make the transfer system better (a sore point right now, your youth academy and scouting are essentially pointless), I do hope this gets looked at.

My main point of frustration with this game, however, is having moved onto the higher difficulties, the game starts to utilise scripting, when the probabilities start going wack mysteriously more often ([i] especially [/i] when one of the only stats the game purports to show you is probabilities in the first place!), rather than the having the AI make smarter decisions. It truly is wild just how often suddenly you'll find that your side will stop hitting the low health target with a 40% presence, or the enemy repeatedly beats the odds and keeps attacking your carry with a 8% presence. There are 3 core things holding this game back from a recommendation. 

1) Tactics cards:
RNG! 2.5 seasons (15-25 hours of gameplay) until you have the OPTION to manually have access to the cards you need. This hurts the game in a few ways. It restricts players effective hero pools, shrinking the game. Artificially inflating the learning curve and forcing the player into learning bad habits. Which creates an infinite amount of jumping off points. That kind of frustration leaves a bad taste in players mouths and can prematurely put them off the game. And not ever feel the need to return.

2) Scouting players:
RNG! This one is really bad cus they did it well in version 1 of this game. Then they changed it for no reason. And now it is trash. 

Before you could actually scout for traits you'd actually want. Then develop them further into players that can become champions...

Now? Now it's entirely RNG. A gotcha mechanic spits out random players. Then you have to spend, and I kid you not, casino tokens to 'influence' them. fighting every other team in the game for them. Okay. Why not. Ignore scouting. Trade for players you want, if you can afford it.

3) Translation? Not even once.
I've played and understood many Machine Translated games. This game has to be poorly translated on purpose. Everything is nonsensical gibberish. Meaning even the dialogue trees are RNG based.

If these core issues get fixed the game will transform from another shitty casino rouge-lite into one of the best team fighting strategy and management games ever.

There are a few more things that bother me personally.

-Versatility. 
When the game launched players only had access to one trait. So. That is why this goes here instead of being an insurmountable problem. Cus this shit sucks. It is RNG based. Do you have an idea for a player with 3 different play styles to seamlessly assimilate into every meta? To bad. You'll have better luck scouting them then spending 2 seasons bringing their stats up to game speed... Yes. That is a joke. 

-The A.I. 
Playing on hell difficulty. In game 3 of worlds. If the CPU loses here they lose it all. They spend an entire turn playing gathering momentum. Their next deployment phase comes up. 23 strategy points to spend... My butthole puckers. Then the A.I. proceeds to spend all 23 points to move all their players to gank my solo lane... while I had two of their players over-watched. So it was a 3v5... Where they were attacking a player not involved in the objective fight that was happening the same turn... They lost 2 players in that fight. Which caused them to lose the 2v4 for the objective... My Mid lane made 1,500 gold in one turn. And it wasn't even my turn... Causing them to snowball. Giving me the win. Great job devs. Nailed it.

All that nastiness aside. I love this game. While it does fail as a tactical team fight management game. It does succeed as a casino rouge-lite, tactical team fight simulator, simulator. Basically. If you like thinking about playing games as much or more then actually playing the game. This game might be for you.

-The graphics, sound design and U.I. are well done and charming. Yes. There is A.I. art. And what is worse is the fact that not only is it extremely poorly done. It is also completely unnecessary.

-The base heroes are great. A few duds. But with enough foresight and creativity you can turn them into hyper-carries.

-The rest of the management outside of what has already been mentioned is amazing and flawlessly implemented.

-They finally got picks and bands up to a Gold rank moba standard. At least on very hard difficulty. It is genuinely fun now. Before you just banged your head against the wall until your opponent beat themselves.  

-There are about 4 billion options. You can, almost, completely customize your entire experience in this game.

-The newest Rouge-lite mode. ;) It is really good. Player development is based off winning only. No worrying about trophies, KDA or MVP scores. 

-Worlds is meh. The teams in premiere league are so poorly translated their player names just appear as empty boxes. And the World rankings info tab is also glitched to where every player is shown to have lost 99 games, each season, every season. BUT! Tier 4 skills are cool. And being recognized as being #1 is always very nice.

-Building unhinged team comps of the most absurd heroes. Then going 90-0. The synergies and counter-play in this game is spot on... I just wish the CPU understood more of it.

Fin:
If you love spreadsheets, senseless min/maxing, and/or theory crafting. AND don't mind having the game continuously demean and disrespect your time and intelligence. Then you could consider picking this game up on a severe discount. If you are looking for a fun, casual single player MOBA experience. This ain't it chief. This game is less strategy and tactics. And more RNG and risk management. 

P.S. DEFINITELY Ignore the DLC's. I bought the 1st one and immediately turned it off. Lazy, thoughtless greed. Heroes and items thrown at the player that don't fit in the game. They feel like they are from a different studio. It is bad. One of the heroes has an ability that just feeds me free kills while costing the CPU 6 sp. Foso's Libra record against me is 0 kills for her to 17 free kills for me... Working as intended devs? I literally never use any of the heroes. They are unimaginative and sucky. ew. gross.

ive got a lot of feelings about FACEMINER. its a game that makes you think on several very prevalent issues in our modern society. but the game itself can feel like a bit of a drag to actually play.

FACEMINER is a very blatant criticism of ai usage and the effects of ai usage, like the environmental and economic factors. theres also themes of cyber security, specifically once you unlock the ability to purchase facefinder cameras to harvest your own data. the game itself is an interesting form of criticism.

the story is heavily told through the various emails you receive. most of the emails are incredibly short. some are messages from the FACEMINER administration on things like work efficiency or claiming the negative effects are just fearmongering. other emails are from other FACEMINER employees discussing the ethics and effects of their work. a lot of emails provide nothing to the story, just standard emails about mundane stuff. its both an interesting and incredibly boring method of story telling. 

its interesting in the way that it allows you to see into the lives of your fellow coworkers. some seem to be hysterical and outraged at anyone who opposes their work, others fearful of the world theyre creating others are jaded and dont seem to care. these are all very real responses to the usage of ai in modern society, so i definitely think it was important to be included. however, your inbox very quickly gets full of messages. notices about efficiency or expenses, rank up emails, babbling between employees, messages from people opposing the work of FACEMINER, etc. it all just gets jumbled up. and since the inbox is the method of storytelling, all this nonsensical data makes it hard to keep track of the story. 

the gameplay loop is also a bit boring. you can select how fast you want your game to go or if you want to play an endless game. even on the quicker speed, the game still takes ages to actually reach the ending. and endless isn’t even all that fun– it’s the same exact game, just without an ending. there’s no new infrastructure or offsets to switch things up. which, gets frustrating even in a standard run. things get more expensive exponentially. it’s really easy to dig yourself into a financial pit or to basically keep your game at a standstill. 

one major bone to pick is that you have to pay to save your game. you get a free autosave after ranking up, but in order to save, you need to pay. and like all other upgrades in the game, saving becomes exponentially more expensive the more saves you make. it’s honestly just a nuisance.

the game does use ai for image generation. specifically, all datasets are made up of ai-generated faces. it uses nvidia’s ffhq dataset to generate these faces. while the devs claim it’s for thematic purposes (as well as it would obviously be tough and expensive to legally gather enough faces to create the datasets). but how many of the people whose faces were used in nvidia’s dataset consented to their faces being used? and since the ai is trained on real people who may or may not have consented to their images being used for ai training, it undermines the criticisms the game it trying to make. at least, in my opinion. the game’s whole point is to criticise ai usage through the unethical gathering of data and the effects it has on the world. if the game’s face data was gathered unethically, then FACEMINER has become what it set out to criticise. it ‘s a slippery slope.

all in all, a summary of the story is just “ai bad”. do i think it’s got a good story? yes, if you’re willing to do some digging to read the important emails. do i think it’s fun? no, not really. once you’ve made it to mid-/late-game, you’ve done basically everything but get the story’s finale. most late-game features, such as the emissions/offsets have barely any upgrades. if you’re interested in the criticisms this game has on ai and a cynical worldview, then maybe you’d enjoy the game. but it’s definitely a type of game you dont actively play, you just check in every now and then to upgrade it and let it run on its own.

Overall, this game delivers on its promises: you can farm and drive licensed tractors. So far, so good.

But oh boy, the rest of it is just a disgrace of low-effort incompetence and neglect you’d expect in a license-filled slop game. This wouldn’t be so bad if this weren’t the fourth—or maybe third—installment in this series.

The menus are a hacky compromise to avoid making their own PC/console UI, meaning that on PC, navigating them—for example, looking at mods—is a pain-inducing experience. The constant reminder of what each button does is also heavily oriented toward consoles. In-game, this continues, but I give it a pass since there’s a lot of stuff to control.

In-game, the next big thing you will encounter is performance. It’s called “(20)25” but has so little modern optimization, and it runs only on one core. So even if you have a monster, beefy machine to run this, you will have bad performance, lags, and spikes. It’s horrendous how badly this thing runs on modern hardware.

The overall gameplay is also plagued with console controls. The map is a mystery that I think is basically not properly finished, and controlling AI workers is a pain. But as far as I’ve read, they are already far better than in previous installments.

The driving physics are passable but sometimes feel really shit due to performance hitches, and they often do not behave either like a simulator or a casual driving experience. Wheels won’t return to neutral positions, for example—but sometimes they do. Oversteering with keyboard and mouse is a constant struggle.

Multiplayer works, but also rather badly—and even consumer-hostile. If you want to host your own private dedicated server, you need to buy an additional license, as the game prevents you from running the game twice or downloading the server separately like 99% of other games allow. This is the biggest and unforgivable flaw. This is something I have not encountered yet in any game I’ve played and hosted myself! Oh, and of course there is no Linux server either; it all must be run under Windows, which eats performance. Really shitty product.

One thing that really stands out, however, is the enormous amount of mods this game has and is able to run. We did a test run with over 2,500 mods for additional vehicles and stuff, and it ran no worse than with 450 mods—or none. This is really cool!

All in all, the overall pain we had before even starting to play, and the constant reminders and bad experiences while playing, clearly make me not recommend this “product.”

Sengoku Dynasty – When "Dynasty" Means Downgrade

If you ever wondered what Medieval Dynasty would be like if it lost a bet and had to wear its cousin's hand-me-downs, welcome to Sengoku Dynasty! It takes everything its older sibling did… and does it slightly worse. Every. Single. Thing.

Let’s break it down:

Graphics? Imagine Medieval Dynasty but after eating some bad sushi. The textures feel like they took a vow of simplicity, and the lighting makes me wonder if feudal Japan was just permanently overcast.

Mechanics? Think Medieval Dynasty, but with all the screws a little loose. Movement feels off, combat is about as smooth as a rice field in a drought, and every action seems like it needs an extra step—because, why not?

Building? I hope you enjoy watching your character struggle to place structures in the most unintuitive way possible! In Medieval Dynasty, building was a pleasure. Here, it’s more of a meditation exercise in patience.

Combat? If you’ve ever wanted to fight enemies with the intensity of two drunk samurais trying to swat a fly, this is your game. The AI attacks with the coordination of a toddler wielding a broom.

Story? There is one…  But like a missing katana in the mud, it’s hard to find and even harder to care about.

Despite all of this, the game could be fun if you enjoy open-world survival and have a high tolerance for jank. Maybe one day with enough patches, Sengoku Dynasty will be worthy of the “Dynasty” name. But for now, it feels like the "bargain-bin" edition of its predecessor.

Final Verdict: 5/10 – Needs more honor and polish.

Class identity? What's that? let's just make it so all classes can use everything and have practically 0 reason to ever specialise, it's not like the perks were made for that reason, they were just a vague suggestion clearly. All of the skills feel next to useless minus the few meta ones - why add more if they're all garbage? 3 trees and yet most of them are not even worth looking at.

Core gameplay changes were done, such as removing the weight and thus the inventory system entirely, which helped balancing out the powerful weapons and gave you a reason to think about what you took (on top of choosing things that your perk actually benefited from - but whatever...) wave lengths are gone, now it's always 6 wave, no 4/7/10 anymore - Endless? Objective?(not that I cared for it, but usually sequels should probably have more in it) all MIA. Healing? limited to a certain usage based on skills however this means that battles of attrition will always end in failure since you're limited on how much damage you can take, this also means healing others is exclusively medic weapons now for darts, I don't get this change - why attempt to fix what wasn't broken?

Graphically, colours are all washed out, nothing really pops and things can blend together, I don't mind the visual changes on the zeds, but I hate how grey everything appears, it's completely lifeless.

Map design is probably the only thing I don't hate, the maps all feel nice and somebody even remade them in KF2 which lets you enjoy them without the drag of having to play them in their original state.

I should also note that I had 0 ability to finish a multiplayer match because community servers are gone and so are dedicated servers, because we still live in 2007 apparently and I kept disconnecting before any match could even finish. So all my playtime was done solo, which led me thinking that maybe weapons feel so horrible because zed hp isn't scaled, but even then, that means they still feel like shit with multiple players. Community stuff in general is completely absent, I don't think we'll see community skins make a return - mutators are out and goodbye to custom maps I guess. Will they return? who knows and who cares, something tells me this game won't have anybody developing for it anyway.

While there's certainly more to expand on, I'm trying to keep my complaining brief - but last thing I need to touch on is the bosses. They're boring and they have 0 personality. The only real time you need to dodge is to avoid the Fleshpounds and their tracking slam attacks and Gorefast stabs, because even if you sidestep before they even start it, they always seem to connect, but whatever - skill issue.

So... yeah. Wait on it for a couple years and come back to an amazing game? Fat chance, I'd wager now this game will be completely abandoned within a year once the team gets axed for it's poor sales. I almost want to recommend *Faceminer*, but the question isn’t “can you play it” so much as “should you?” Up front, it has an interesting premise and a bit of charm. The retro interface feels authentic and gives the impression the game might develop into something deeper. But the gameplay automates almost immediately and never evolves, creating an incremental idler that plateaus within an hour. The story tries to build mystery around who wants these faces mined and why, but it never really pays off that curiosity in either answers or impulse.

*Universal Paperclips* is the closest comparison: both games are about destroying the world through automating a single mindless task. Beyond that, the difference is obvious. *Paperclips* begins with a single button and keeps evolving—each new stage shifts the goalposts until you sit atop your throne of paperclips and realize how far you’ve gone in destroying everything to achieve it. *Faceminer* wants to tell a similar story about obsession and exploitation, but it gives away the moral upfront and never lets the mechanics mirror that descent. You’re told mining faces is bad from the start, so there’s no arc—just repetition. And mining faces isn’t fun to begin with, so why is anyone doing it?

The result is a game that looks clever but feels hollow. Its metaphor for crypto and AI collapses under its own contradictions, asking you to balance progress with environmental guilt in a system that insists you stop. Once you understand the point—and you will, because it’s endlessly repeated—there’s nothing left to play for. It’s a neat idea trapped in a loop that proves its own message: not playing really is the winning move.  And so, can I really recommend a game that actively insists you don't play it?

Chernobylite 2... So, as a backer for both the original Chernobylite and now its sequel, Chernobylite 2, I was super hyped for this early access release. I even got to play the "pre-launch" version, which actually ran a bit better overall. Honestly, though, that excitement's been a bit tough to hold onto. This review's coming out a bit late because when the game first launched, I just couldn't play it – the performance issues were really rough.

Fast forward almost three months, and while the game is technically playable now, it's still pretty rough around the edges when it comes to performance. It's a real bummer, honestly, because I had such high hopes for it.

Diving into the actual gameplay, it's a bit of a mixed bag. The melee combat feels like it's trying to be a bit like Dark Souls but maybe missed some of the key ingredients, and everything feels really fast-paced. As for gunplay, it's okay, but it just doesn't have that satisfying, weighty feel that made shooting in the first Chernobylite so great.

The classes are decent, though many of them do feel a bit similar. I have to give a huge shoutout to the Chernomancer, though – that one is genuinely unique and a ton of fun! It's basically your magic-user but with all these cool mutant abilities, which is a really fresh idea.

So, even though I haven't been able to sink a ton of hours into it yet, I wanted to share my initial thoughts for anyone considering picking it up. Right now, in its current state, I'd probably suggest holding off for a bit.

The game feels like it's trying too hard to be Elden Ring, when it really should be leaning into a STALKER 2-style experience. I'm hoping for a shift in direction at some point, aiming for more of a shooter RPG vibe, much like STALKER.

However, I really do believe in Farm 51. They've shown a great commitment to their games in the past, and I'm optimistic that they know what they're doing. I have a strong feeling that in about six months or more, this game could really transform into something special. So, if you're interested, I'd highly recommend adding it to your wishlist and checking back on it later in the year.

As a big fan of the STALKER series, this franchise means a lot to me. I'm really looking forward to seeing how Farm 51 continues to develop the game in the coming years, and I'll definitely be updating this review as things progress!

Let this intro serve as not just a warning to potential buyers but a message to the developers and also provide some context for my early access review:

Chernobylite was my GOTY for 2021 until Inscryption dropped and stole the gold. Get Even was a fantastic story driven stealth shooter with a really cool gameplay hook as well. The Farm 51 always approach their games with a clear vision and the final result is every time something unique and worthwhile. However, Chernobylite 2 SHOULD ONLY BE PLAYED/PURCHASED by those of you interested in supporting the devs during early access either financially or by playing and providing your own unique feedback. There are just too many issues both technical and gameplay related that will only serve to frustrate players. To sum it up as simply as possible: this game makes a terrible first impression which combined with the Early Access tag can bury a game. Pros and Cons incoming. Cons will include genuine feedback but I will add any additional feedback after the list of cons.

PROS:
- Choice between 1st and 3rd person perspective allows players to choose their preferred method of play 
- Voice acting is nearly on par with previous games from the devs (although some of the dialogue sounds like placeholder AI, which shouldn't be looked at as a con for Early Access, please stop chewing on your keyboard)
- Base building is even better and more expansive than the first game and I can only imagine what a fully decked out base would look like (seriously addicting)
- Melee combat is surprisingly smooth and feels not only functional but a viable way to approach many combat encounters. Although the input queue will definitely trip up some of the button spammers out there (I played in 1st person).
- Worldbuilding is strong and plays off the foundation set by the first game very well.
- Great OST, on par with the first in terms of tone and style. Not sure if it's the same composer as the first game, but there is a reason I bought the OST for the first one and I will buy this one as well if it lives up to that in the end.

CONS
- Tons of graphical issues. You name it and the game probably has it. I don't mind this stuff for Early Access, but it reaches a point where your immersion is just obliterated making it nearly impossible to really stay in the game.
- Some key rebinding doesn't actually work, which combined with inconsistent tutorialization can make it difficult to figure out what some buttons do. Seriously, during the tutorial section when you're trying out the classes (which ends up being basically meaningless when you make your class choice) I thought I was doing something incorrectly because the NPC kept saying I was doing something wrong no matter what I did during the encounter which made me second guess how the weapons actually worked.
- Deeper distinction between classes (which may or may not come later in the game). The RPG choices presented to certain classes don't seem very interesting or intuitive. And it looks like any class can use basically any gear with no penalty? 
- There is very little feedback for anything that you do outside of swinging a melee weapon. I didn't even know I leveled until I got back to the base because there is no sound or music or fanfare whatsoever. For how absurdly overbearing the UI can be, the fact that it didn't tell me I had leveled in any meaningful way just felt so strange.
- Speaking of UI, somehow the building elements from the first game (building stations like healing, ammo crafting, etc.) were made more difficult because of how little of your screen you can actually utilize when placing a station. If there is a button to minimize or remove UI during that process I didn't see it (and I'm willing to just be dumb on this one) but the fact that either wasn't obvious, or just set as the default is incredibly frustrating. This was exacerbated further by the incredibly poor lighting in the base itself. I don't mind low lighting when you're out exploring (in the first game especially it made for some incredibly tense moments), but for the building stuff, you should either just have better visibility by default OR the building should just be moved into the base building menu as well. Other than porting over the elements from the first game for the sake of ease, I can't imagine why this wasn't just a change that was made in general.
- This is probably my biggest criticism of the game and I don't think it is necessarily an Early Access issue so please take special noteL The enemy types are far too varied mechanically to look so similar. The ones that shoot look like the ones that swing look like the ones that punch. I don't mind them all looking so similar, it makes sense in the lore and it would be weird to change it too much, but something has to be considered. If you're standing in green grass near trees and a Chernobylite deposit with 4 or 5 Chernohosts that all look identical but you can't tell which one is firing at you while another one swings, that's just not a good approach to enemy design. There are far too many examples of this done right to fail this hard.

I may update my review with additional feedback when there are major changes, but as it stands I may not come back until 1.0 so I can experience the world and story as intended and not with so many issues. I have no doubt whatsoever that the final product can absolutely be one of the best RPGs on Steam. Even in its current state (2 days into Early Access) it is superior to mainstream garbage like Starfield, But I want newcomers to get the best that the team at The Farm 51 are capable of. So in the meantime, I would recommend either replaying OR playing for the first time the original Chernobylite. A fantastic game from fantastic developers and by the time you get through that one, the second one might be in a more acceptable state.

From a gameplay perspective, this is a fantastic game with excellent sound design, music, and, I would say, atmosphere—though I can’t fully experience it. You’d expect a game set in what’s essentially an empty void with scattered islands to run well, but the reality is quite the opposite.

I encountered performance issues even with the demo. Granted, I run the game at 1440p, but even on the lowest settings, I could only manage an average of 40-50 FPS. Performance would frequently dip even lower when exploring or when more islands came into view. While the developers have made significant improvements since the demo, the performance is still far from acceptable. For a game that appears so lightweight, this level of optimization is, frankly, disappointing.

As much as I love the game’s concept and unique design, I sadly can’t give it a positive review in its current state. The only way I managed to achieve a stable 60-70 FPS was through AI frame generation—which is hardly a real fix. Without further optimizations, the performance remains a major drawback to an otherwise incredible experience.

The game starts off promising, but it quickly turns into an exhausting grind with no real sense of progression.

Even after hiring employees, you're still doing 90% of the work yourself. Their presence barely improves efficiency — for example, to wash a car, you still have to drive it to the wash bay, assign the employee, and then wait 2–3 real-time minutes for them to finish. The same goes for every step of the process: you must meet with the seller, buy the car, personally drive it to the mechanic (who only works if you already have the needed parts), then wait another 3 minutes for repairs. Then it's off to the body shop for another 3-minute rust removal and repaint job, followed by the car wash again, then the photo booth, and finally to the sales area. After all that, you still need to go into the office and manually register the car for sale.

None of this can be automated or delegated, and every single vehicle goes through this same drawn-out routine. Meanwhile, once the store is open, you can sell 5 cars in under 5 minutes — meaning your lot is constantly empty because prepping even one car is such a time sink.

This game feels like busywork disguised as simulation. There's no real management here — just repetitive manual labor, stretched out by timers. It’s more tedious than fun.

If you’re like me and enjoy simulator games, trust me — there are better options out there.

I really wanted to like this game, but I couldn't really get into it after trying to fly around for a few hours and testing a few of the mechanics. I usually LOVE plane games, but this one left a bad taste in my mouth in a few ways.

The main mechanic of the game, the flying, feels poorly designed.
- If you use any rudder or elevator AT ALL, your speed tanks. Not sure if this is supposed to be more percentage based, but at the moment of writing this, you loose just as much speed at 1% rudder as you do at full.
- Speed feels off in more ways than one. I know you're literally flying a boat, but when the speedometer shows 350 KNOTS (which is faster than some fighter planes in WWII) and you still feel like you're moving slow, then I'm not sure what is going on.
- On the note of speed, the faster you go the more rotation you gain while using your control surfaces. Probably realistic, but playing on a controller was hard on its own. Not sure what playing on keyboard would be like as I didn't dare try. Maybe cutting down on the input curve for the rotation speed would help the player?
- The boost is cool, but you literally lose control of your aircraft while doing so. If you make the mistake of pulling up while boosting, you might just enter a perpetual loop that you cannot escape. I crashed a couple of times like this with different pilots.
- Overall, I felt like the flying became a second thought over all the other strange and offputting mechanics in the game. I'm glad I never got into a dogfight. I doubt I would be able to do anything of note.

I have a few gripes about the UI as well.
- It feels largely unintuitive and is clunky to get around. I started using the controller to get around, but quickly realized it was nearly impossible to figure out which button the game was focusing on.
- Even with mouse and keyboard I had to press some buttons multiple times in order for them to do something. Was this due to the controller having a button selected somehow?
- Inventory management was fine, but left something to be desired. You have so little space in your plane, you can fit a few apples and a few grapes in there, which you can bring back to make brews with, but overall I felt like going back and forth 3 times to make one batch is too much with how the flying feels.

* I cannot say this for sure, but the VOs almost sound like AI? It sounds a bit unnatural sometimes. Not hating on the VOs at all if that's not the case. It's mostly the end of some of the sentences where the tone sounds weird. *


Overall, all I can say is this. In the current state of the game, if you're looking for a nice flight based exploration game, this is not it. If they fixed the controls and feel of the plane, then perhaps.
